summary: Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneer in artificial intelligence, quit Google to speak freely about AI's dangers, warning that computers could become smarter than people sooner than expected. He expressed concerns about AI creating convincing false images and texts, making it hard to know what is true, and displacing workers. The article also includes reactions from experts calling for AI regulation.

claims.text: Geoffrey Hinton quit Google to speak freely about AI dangers without considering how it impacts Google.
claims.evidence_quote: I left so that I could talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google

claims.text: Hinton worried that AI could create convincing false images and texts, leading to a world where people cannot know what is true anymore.
claims.evidence_quote: not be able to know what is true anymore

claims.text: Hinton said it is hard to see how to prevent bad actors from using AI for bad things.
claims.evidence_quote: It is hard to see how you can prevent the bad actors from using it for bad things

claims.text: Hinton previously thought AI could become smarter than people in 30 to 50 years or longer, but no longer thinks that.
claims.evidence_quote: I thought it was 30 to 50 years or even longer away. Obviously, I no longer think that.

claims.text: Hinton denied quitting to criticize Google and said Google acted very responsibly.
claims.evidence_quote: Google itself had "acted very responsibly" and denied that he had quit so that he could criticise his former employer.

claims.text: Google's chief scientist Jeff Dean said the company remains committed to a responsible approach to AI.
claims.evidence_quote: We remain committed to a responsible approach to A.I. We’re continually learning to understand emerging risks while also innovating boldly.

claims.text: Since OpenAI released ChatGPT in November, generative AI applications have provoked concern over future regulation.
claims.evidence_quote: Since Microsoft-backed startup OpenAI released ChatGPT in November, the growing number of "generative AI" applications that can create text or images have provoked concern over the future regulation of the technology.

claims.text: Dr Carissa Veliz, an associate professor at Oxford, said the time to regulate AI is now.
claims.evidence_quote: The time to regulate AI is now.

claims.text: The technology could quickly displace workers and become a greater danger as it learns new behaviours.
claims.evidence_quote: The technology could quickly displace workers, and become a greater danger as it learns new behaviours.
